sentences.text: Most passing arrangements on the Intracoastal today are made on VHF, and the two rule books treat that differently.
Under the Inland rules, a vessel that reaches agreement by radiotelephone isn’t obliged to sound the whistle signals, though she still may.
But if agreement isn’t reached, whistle signals shall be exchanged in good time, and the whistle signals prevail.
Those calls are usually made on channel thirteen, the bridge-to-bridge channel.
Under the International rules, there’s no such exemption.
So picture yourself offshore, beyond the demarcation line.
You and a freighter agree on the radio to pass port to port, and you turn to starboard.
Do you still sound one short blast?
Offshore, the radio never replaces the whistle.
Short is one second, prolonged is four to six.
One, two, three: starboard, port, astern.
International signals tell, Inland signals ask.
And five short blasts means doubt.
Next time: fog signals and distress signals.
